neighbours.label: Stranded, stressed do / does / did in a spoken reply ('Yeah, it does', 'you do'): the auxiliary ending the clause, with its verb left out; do-support before a verb and main-verb do stay low.
fire: “Does the knee still bother you?” “Yeah, it does,” he told me.
Mike: I guess that matters to people. Anna: It does, yeah, it really does.
“You look exactly like your mother.” “Yeah, I do,” she laughed.
“Do these two know each other?” “Oh, they do,” he said.
Kate: It sounds kind of risky to me. Tom: Yeah, it does.
“He loves that old truck.” “He sure does,” I said.
“Did she call you back?” “Yes, she did,” he said quietly.
“You always say that.” “Well, I do,” she answered with a grin.
quiet: “Does the knee still bother you?” “Only on stairs,” he told me.
Mike: I guess that matters to people. Anna: We do care about it, yeah.
“You look exactly like your mother.” “Yeah, people say that,” she laughed.
“Do these two know each other?” “Oh, they do business,” he said.
Kate: It sounds kind of risky to me. Tom: Yeah, risky is right.
“He loves that old truck.” “He does love it,” I said slowly.
“Did she call you back?” “Yes, she did call,” he said quietly.
“You always say that.” “Well, I do mean it,” she answered with a grin.
